\chapter{Dog and Cat}
\label{ch:ml-dog-and-cat}
\hlchaptermodality{21}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a dog and a cat in Malayalam.}

Say nāya on the shared Dravidian dog-root, then pūcha, which follows Tamil's cat-word rather than Kannada's.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ml{നായ}, \ml{പൂച്ച}]{\ml{നായ}, \ml{പൂച്ച} — matching Tamil closely on both counts}

\label{lesson:ML-C21-naaya-poocha}



\begin{quote}
Malayalam keeps close company with its nearest cousin, Tamil, on both words this time — while still fitting into the honest, more fragmented Dravidian picture for \textquotedblleft{}cat.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{നായ}} (\emph{nāya}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{dog}\textquotedblright{}) continues the same solid, native \textbf{Proto-Dravidian} root as Kannada's \textbf{\ka{ನಾಯಿ}} (\emph{nāyi}) and Tamil's own word — no mystery here at all, unlike the tangled dog-words of Spanish, Hindi, and English.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{പൂച്ച}} (\emph{pūcha}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{cat}\textquotedblright{}) closely matches Tamil's \textbf{everyday} word for cat — a different root from Kannada's \textbf{\ka{ಬೆಕ್ಕು}} (\emph{bekku}, related instead to the word for \textquotedblleft{}wildcat\textquotedblright{}) and Telugu's \textbf{\te{పిల్లి}} (\emph{pilli}, a separate Proto-Dravidian root of its own, most likely the source behind Sanskrit's \emph{biḍāla} and Hindi's \emph{billī}). So \textquotedblleft{}cat\textquotedblright{} genuinely splits three ways across just these four Dravidian languages, even though \textquotedblleft{}dog\textquotedblright{} mostly agrees.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāya\textquotedblright{} — dog, same solid root as Kannada and Tamil
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pūcha\textquotedblright{} — cat, matching Tamil's everyday word closely
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \textbf{\ml{നായ}} share Kannada's \emph{nāyi} root? (\textbf{Yes} — the same solid, native Proto-Dravidian root.) Does \textbf{\ml{പൂച്ച}} match Kannada's \emph{bekku} or Tamil's everyday cat-word? (\textbf{Tamil's} — Kannada's \emph{bekku} and Telugu's \emph{pilli} both come from different roots entirely.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sa]{\ml{സ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S124-letter-sa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ദ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{സ}}
\textbf{\ml{സ}} — \emph{sa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{s}, it is \textbf{sa}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ml{സ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{നമസ്കാരം}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}} \emph{santōṣam} — joy / pleased to meet you
  \item \textbf{\ml{സുഖം}} \emph{sukhaṁ} — well-being — and the reply "\ml{സുഖമാണ്}
  \item \textbf{\ml{സാരമില്ല}} \emph{sāramilla} — it doesn't matter / no problem / you're welcome
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{സ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{സ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ml{സ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ml{നമസ്കാരം}  ·  \ml{സന്തോഷം}  ·  \ml{നന്ദി}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ml{സ} three times, saying \emph{sa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ml{സ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ml{സ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{sa}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
